paragraphs: This paper approaches interpretation by asking how groups of input features contribute information to a network’s decision function. The motivation is that a deep network can combine many input elements through complicated relationships, making its predictions difficult to explain. The proposed framework measures feature contributions using functional entropy, connecting interpretation to a mathematical description of the network’s behavior with respect to its input.

The key theoretical tool is the log-Sobolev inequality. It bounds functional entropy using functional Fisher information while accounting for the covariance of the data. This relationship provides a principled basis for assigning information contributions to a subset of features. The explanation therefore concerns how features participate in the decision function, with data covariance explicitly included in the formulation.

Experiments cover images, text, and audio. The authors report that their approach outperforms existing sampling-based interpretation methods across these different signals. These results support the usefulness of the framework beyond a single input type, while the mathematical contribution supplies a common foundation for measuring feature information.
icml-2022-a-functional-information-persp.tldr: The paper uses functional information measures to explain feature contributions and reports improvements over sampling-based interpretation methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies how several agents can jointly control a dynamical system while adapting to disturbances. The system’s dynamics are assumed known, but disturbances may be adversarial. Each agent starts with a stabilizing controller. The objective is to achieve effective distributed control without relying on a centralized joint policy computed in advance.

The main contribution is a reduction that converts a standard regret-minimizing control method into a distributed algorithm. Regret compares the algorithm’s accumulated performance with that of an optimal precomputed joint policy. The reduction preserves a low-regret guarantee against this benchmark. To establish it, the authors extend online convex optimization to multiple agents and apply tools developed for single-agent nonstochastic control.

The empirical evaluation uses a model of an overactuated aircraft. In that setting, the distributed method demonstrates robustness to failure and adversarial changes in the dynamics. Together, the theory and experiments support distributed adaptation as a viable approach under the paper’s control setup: agents can respond during operation while retaining a performance comparison with a coordinated policy.
icml-2022-a-regret-minimization-approach.tldr: A reduction turns regret-minimizing control methods into distributed controllers with low regret against an optimal precomputed joint policy.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to send for labeling. Requesting labels in batches reduces the number of interactions with a labeling oracle, which may be a person. However, the learner cannot use answers from within a batch to revise its remaining selections. This reduced adaptivity can make batch selection statistically less effective.

The paper studies the pool-based setting, where all unlabeled candidate examples are available beforehand. It proposes a stage-wise greedy algorithm that carefully balances informativeness and diversity. This balance addresses two needs at once: selecting points that are useful for learning and selecting a batch whose contents provide sufficiently varied information. The contribution includes a theoretical analysis of this selection strategy.

The authors show that excess risk, expressed as a function of the number of requested labels, matches known minimax rates in standard statistical learning settings. Their results also have a mild dependence on batch size. This provides a rigorous account of how balancing information and diversity can support statistically effective learning while reducing interactions with the labeling oracle.
icml-2022-achieving-minimax-rates-in-poo.tldr: A stage-wise batch selection algorithm balances informativeness and diversity to achieve known minimax learning rates with mild batch-size dependence.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a physics-based environment in which agents assemble connectable magnetic blocks into a sequence of target structures. Although the pieces and objective are simple, combining blocks into different blueprints creates a large range of possible structures. Successful assembly requires planning over multiple steps, reasoning about physical behavior, and coordinating two hands.

The training approach combines large-scale reinforcement learning with graph-based policies. Graph representations provide structure for the policy’s decisions in this assembly setting. The authors find that this combination is effective without additional complexity: trained agents can build complex blueprints they have never encountered, without further training on those targets.

The agents also operate in a reset-free setting even though they were not specifically trained for it. Extensive experiments examine the roles of training scale, structured representations, learning across multiple tasks, and curricula. The findings identify assembly as both a useful robotics objective and a diagnostic setting for studying how embodied agents acquire skills that transfer across varied construction problems.
icml-2022-blocks-assemble-learning-to-as.tldr: Large-scale reinforcement learning with graph-based policies produces block-assembly agents that generalize to unseen blueprints and operate without resets.

paragraphs: This paper investigates contextual bandits with linear payoffs, where decisions use observed context and learning is measured through regret. Its central distinction is between adversarially chosen contexts and stochastic contexts. While the former setting has a square-root-in-time lower bound, the authors prove an instance-independent polylogarithmic regret result for the stochastic setting they study.

Their algorithm, LR-SCB, combines estimation of the payoff parameters with regret minimization. It works in epochs: estimates obtained in one epoch help reduce regret in the next. The method uses a norm-adaptive algorithm to exploit the parameter estimates, and its analysis examines how shifting a linear contextual bandit problem affects regret.

The result shows that the way contexts arise can substantially change the achievable learning rate. Under the paper’s stochastic-context setting, regret can grow polylogarithmically with the number of decisions instead of following the square-root dependence associated with arbitrary contexts. Experiments also show regret scaling consistent with the polylogarithmic behavior, supporting the theoretical distinction between these context settings.
icml-2022-breaking-the-sqrtt-barrier-ins.tldr: LR-SCB exploits stochastic contexts to achieve instance-independent polylogarithmic regret in the contextual linear bandit setting studied.

paragraphs: This paper compares two ways of handling rotations in images defined on a sphere. One builds rotational equivariance into the network architecture through S2CNNs. The other trains standard convolutional networks with increasing amounts of data augmentation. The comparison uses baseline architectures and images containing one or several MNIST or FashionMNIST items projected onto a sphere.

The results depend on the task. For classification, the desired label stays the same when an image rotates. Standard networks can reach at least the performance of the equivariant network when their size and the amount of augmentation increase considerably. In these experiments, augmentation and additional model capacity can therefore compensate for the architectural difference.

For semantic segmentation, the output must move consistently with the rotated input. Here, equivariant networks consistently outperform the standard networks while using significantly fewer parameters. The paper also compares training time and inference latency. These measurements help frame the practical choice around task behavior, model size, and computation rather than accuracy alone.
icml-2022-equivariance-versus-augmentati.tldr: On spherical-image tasks, augmentation can close the classification gap, while equivariant networks retain a clear segmentation advantage.

paragraphs: Evaluating adversarial robustness requires attacks that can reliably expose a model’s weaknesses. The paper identifies computational cost as a major obstacle to using AutoAttack, particularly when resources are limited or adversarial examples must be generated during training. It proposes the minimum-margin attack as a faster way to perform this evaluation.

The method evaluates candidate adversarial examples through the margin between two targets. The authors use this quantity to identify the most adversarial candidate. A second component, Sequential TArget Ranking Selection, makes target selection efficient and keeps the attack’s cost independent of the number of classes. These components address the quality of the selected examples and the expense of finding them.

Across extensive experiments, the minimum-margin attack achieves performance comparable to AutoAttack while requiring only 3% of its computational time. This is an empirical comparison from the reported evaluations. The result supports using the method both to assess robustness with fewer resources and to generate high-quality adversarial examples within adversarial training.
icml-2022-fast-and-reliable-evaluation-o.tldr: The minimum-margin attack matches AutoAttack’s reported evaluation performance using 3% of its computational time in the paper’s experiments.

paragraphs: Privacy accounting computes the privacy parameters that result when mechanisms are used together or repeatedly. This paper introduces a numerical algorithm for composing privacy random variables, with the goal of calculating accurate differential privacy parameters efficiently. Its contribution concerns the computational resources needed for this accounting task.

For repeating the same mechanism k times, the algorithm requires time and memory that grow polylogarithmically in k. The guarantee applies to a broad class of mechanisms, including the subsampled Gaussian mechanism used in analyses of differentially private stochastic gradient descent. The cited previous approach required roughly square-root growth in running time for this repeated-mechanism task, up to logarithmic factors.

The approach also handles compositions of k different mechanisms from the same class. In that case, it improves the stated time and memory dependence from approximately k to the power 1.5 to approximately linear in k, again suppressing logarithmic factors. These results make accurate numerical accounting more computationally efficient for both repeated and varied mechanisms, with the strongest improvement applying to self-composition.
icml-2022-faster-privacy-accounting-via-.tldr: A numerical privacy-accounting algorithm achieves polylogarithmic time and memory for repeated composition of mechanisms from a broad class.

paragraphs: Gaussian smoothing supports optimization when derivatives are unavailable by perturbing the current parameters and using objective evaluations to estimate a gradient. Its usual perturbations come from a standard normal distribution. This paper asks whether changing that sampling distribution can improve the gradient estimate while retaining the same computational complexity.

The authors analyze derivative-free optimization of nonconvex functions and choose perturbation distributions according to the mean squared error of the resulting gradient estimate. They derive three distributions with provably smaller estimation error than Gaussian smoothing. This makes the perturbation distribution an explicit part of the optimization design, with a mathematical criterion for choosing it.

Evaluations cover linear regression, reinforcement learning, and derivative-free optimization benchmarks. The proposed distributions improve on Gaussian smoothing without increasing computational complexity. They are also competitive with, and usually outperform, Guided ES and Orthogonal ES in the reported evaluations. Those alternatives adapt the covariance of Gaussian perturbations at greater computational cost, making the results evidence that changing the sampling family itself can be useful.
icml-2022-generalizing-gaussian-smoothin.tldr: Three alternative perturbation distributions reduce gradient-estimation error and improve random-search optimization at Gaussian smoothing’s computational complexity.

paragraphs: This paper introduces interchange intervention training, or IIT, to incorporate a chosen causal structure into a neural network while preserving data-driven learning. The starting point is a causal model, such as a deterministic program or Bayesian network. Variables in that model are aligned with representations inside the neural network.

Training compares how the two models behave under matched interventions. For a base input, aligned variables and representations are replaced with the values they would have on a source input. The neural model is then trained to reproduce the causal model’s counterfactual behavior. IIT is fully differentiable and can be combined with other objectives. When its loss is zero, the target causal model is guaranteed to be a causal abstraction of the neural model.

The authors evaluate IIT on structural vision, navigational language, and natural language inference tasks. It achieves the best results in their comparisons with multitask training objectives and data augmentation. The resulting networks also realize the intended causal structure more successfully, giving a concrete behavioral meaning to the claimed improvement in interpretability.
icml-2022-inducing-causal-structure-for-.tldr: IIT trains neural representations to match a target causal model’s intervention behavior, with a causal-abstraction guarantee when its loss reaches zero.

paragraphs: One way to measure a variable’s importance is to compare a model trained on all inputs with a reduced model that excludes that variable. The difficulty is computational: each variable or subset can require another model to be trained. This paper develops a faster approximation to the reduced model for wide neural networks, while also providing statistical guarantees.

The method linearizes the network around the parameters of the already trained full model. A ridge-like penalty makes the approximation problem convex. When this penalty is sufficiently large, the authors prove that their variable-importance estimate has an error rate of O(1/n), where n is the number of training samples. They also establish asymptotic normality, which enables confidence bounds around the estimates.

Simulations show that the approximation is fast and accurate under several data-generating regimes. A seasonal climate forecasting example demonstrates its applicability to a real prediction problem. The contribution therefore combines a cheaper route to reduced-model estimation with tools for expressing uncertainty about the resulting importance measurements.
icml-2022-lazy-estimation-of-variable-im.tldr: A penalized linear approximation avoids full neural-network retraining for variable importance and provides conditional error guarantees and confidence bounds.

paragraphs: Image cartoonization must transfer recognizable style features such as clear edges, smooth shading, and vivid colors. This paper studies cartoonization as unsupervised image-to-image translation with generative adversarial networks. Its central observation is that cartoon texture is especially apparent in certain local image regions, making those regions useful targets for learning the style.

The proposed model adds a region-level adversarial branch alongside the usual image-level branch. A cartoon-texture-saliency sampler adaptively selects patches where the relevant texture is prominent. Training on these patches gives the local branch a focused view of cartoon characteristics, while the image-level branch retains its whole-image role. The approach uses basic adversarial loss to achieve the reported stylization improvements.

Extensive experiments show stronger cartoonization effects, particularly for high-resolution inputs. The authors interpret these results as evidence that directing learning toward texture-salient regions is an important ingredient in cartoon style transfer. The contribution is a concrete training mechanism for making distinctive local style features more visible to adversarial learning.
icml-2022-learning-to-incorporate-textur.tldr: Adaptive sampling of cartoon-texture patches strengthens adversarial cartoonization, with reported benefits especially for high-resolution images.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether deep learning can solve noise-free inverse problems with nearly perfect numerical accuracy. It investigates a computed tomography setting, where the task is to reconstruct an image from measurements. An iterative, end-to-end network produces reconstructions close to numerical precision, comparable to classical compressed sensing strategies in the studied setup.

The method builds on the authors’ winning submission to a sparse-view CT challenge. A distinctive difficulty was that participants did not know the exact forward model describing how the measurements were produced. The approach therefore first estimates the unknown fanbeam geometry through data-driven calibration. This step addresses the measurement model before the reconstruction method is applied.

The paper analyzes its methodology in depth and also reports state-of-the-art performance on the real-world LoDoPaB CT dataset. The near-exact recovery result specifically provides positive evidence for the noise-free inverse-problem question. The additional dataset evaluation establishes a separate practical result, extending the empirical assessment beyond the challenge setup without making near-perfect recovery a universal claim.
icml-2022-near-exact-recovery-for-tomogr.tldr: An iterative network with data-driven geometry calibration achieves near-numerical-precision reconstruction in a noise-free CT setup.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from an existing dataset that may leave important parts of the environment uncertain. Conservative methods address this by avoiding behavior too different from the recorded data. The paper argues that relying exclusively on conservatism can be problematic: results depend on its strength, and conservative objectives can yield highly suboptimal policies.

The authors show that Bayesian-optimal behavior in offline reinforcement learning involves an implicit partially observable decision problem. Under this formulation, an optimal policy must adapt using the transitions observed during evaluation. Its decisions therefore depend on the accumulated interaction history as well as the current state. Experience collected while acting provides information relevant to the uncertainty left by the offline dataset.

The paper presents a model-free algorithm that approximates this adaptive policy and evaluates it on offline reinforcement learning benchmarks. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of training for adaptation. The central implication is that handling uncertainty can involve learning how to respond to new evidence during evaluation, alongside the choices made during offline training.
icml-2022-offline-rl-policies-should-be-.tldr: Bayesian-optimal offline RL requires history-dependent adaptation, motivating a model-free algorithm that learns to use evaluation-time experience.

paragraphs: This paper studies representations for predicting how node attributes change in temporal graphs. It distinguishes two arrangements of graph and sequence processing. The common time-and-graph approach intertwines these operations as the graph evolves. The alternative, called time-then-graph, first represents the histories of nodes and edges, then uses those representations as attributes in a static graph model.

The ordering matters for what the model can express. The authors prove that time-then-graph has an expressivity advantage when both approaches use graph neural networks that are not maximally expressive, including 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman GNNs. This is a conditional comparison tied to the component graph models. It shows that assembling similar types of components differently can change their representational capabilities.

Experiments also find that time-then-graph methods can outperform state-of-the-art time-and-graph methods in both performance and efficiency on some real-world tasks. The paper does not frame this as a universal benchmark victory. Its contribution is to establish the alternative as a theoretically motivated and empirically useful option for temporal graph learning.
icml-2022-on-the-equivalence-between-tem.tldr: Encoding temporal histories before graph processing can improve expressivity under specified GNN conditions and improve performance on some tasks.

paragraphs: Pandora’s Box models search among boxes containing unknown values. The objective combines the cost of opening boxes with the smallest value discovered, so the order of search matters. Min-Sum Set Cover is a special case in which values are either zero or infinity. This paper studies these problems when value vectors arrive online rather than being sampled from a given distribution.

The authors provide a computationally efficient algorithm whose cost is constant-competitive with the optimal search order. This gives a bounded-factor performance comparison for learning the order in the online setting. The result addresses the challenge of making search decisions while the sequence of values is being presented to the learner.

The paper extends the approach to bandit feedback, where each round reveals only the values in boxes that were actually opened. It also treats variants involving the selection of multiple values under a matroid constraint. These extensions broaden the framework to search problems with limited observations and structured restrictions on the selections that are allowed.
icml-2022-online-learning-for-min-sum-se.tldr: An efficient online search algorithm achieves constant competitiveness, with extensions to partial feedback and constrained multiple selections.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a policy using estimated gradients, but noisy estimates can increase the amount of experience needed for learning. This paper addresses that variance problem. After surveying several variance-reduced REINFORCE-type methods, it introduces PAGE-PG, a policy gradient algorithm built around probabilistic gradient estimation.

PAGE-PG switches probabilistically between two kinds of update, producing a loopless method. Its design draws on the PAGE estimator from supervised learning and uses importance sampling to obtain an unbiased gradient estimate. The combination aims to retain the sample-efficiency benefits of variance reduction within a simple update structure.

The authors prove an average sample complexity of O(epsilon^-3) for reaching an epsilon-stationary solution. This matches the most competitive comparison methods under the same setting; the stated target concerns approximate stationarity of the optimization problem. Numerical evaluation on classical control tasks finds competitive performance as well. The contribution is therefore a simpler probabilistic update design that preserves strong theoretical sample complexity and performs competitively in the reported control experiments.
icml-2022-page-pg-a-simple-and-loopless-.tldr: PAGE-PG uses probabilistic updates and importance sampling to match leading variance-reduced policy-gradient sample complexity with a loopless design.

paragraphs: Model inversion for vision produces images from a trained model, but existing techniques often need carefully tuned regularizers to obtain adequate results. The paper highlights total variation and feature regularization as examples whose settings may need to be calibrated separately for each network. This creates practical friction when applying inversion across different image classifiers.

Plug-In Inversion uses a simple set of data augmentations and avoids excessive hyperparameter tuning. Under the proposed scheme, the same augmentation settings can be reused across a wide range of classifiers with different architectures and input dimensions. This reuse is the central practical benefit: the inversion procedure becomes easier to apply across model designs.

The authors demonstrate the approach by inverting Vision Transformers and multilayer perceptrons trained on ImageNet. They describe these demonstrations as previously unaccomplished to the best of their knowledge. The results support the method’s applicability to these architectures and its broader aim of reducing network-specific calibration, while preserving the qualified nature of the paper’s novelty claim.
icml-2022-plug-in-inversion-model-agnost.tldr: Plug-In Inversion uses reusable augmentation settings to invert diverse image classifiers with less model-specific tuning.

paragraphs: Images often need resizing before a machine learning model can process them. This paper treats that scaling procedure as part of the system being attacked. It investigates how weaknesses in resizing interact with weaknesses in the downstream model when an attacker operates in a decision-based black-box setting.

The authors introduce a sampling strategy that allows a black-box attack to exploit the scaling algorithm, scaling defenses, and final model together. This end-to-end view matters because a defense aimed at preprocessing must also withstand attacks that account for the model receiving the processed image. The attack explicitly incorporates these interactions into its search.

Using the scaling-aware attack, the paper finds that most existing scaling defenses are ineffective under the studied downstream-model threat. It also observes that standard black-box attacks can substantially improve their performance by exploiting vulnerable scaling. A demonstration on a commercial Image Analysis API shows the issue in an applied system. The findings support evaluating robustness across the complete image-processing pipeline.
icml-2022-rethinking-image-scaling-attac.tldr: Scaling-aware black-box attacks expose weaknesses arising from the interaction between image resizing, scaling defenses, and downstream models.

paragraphs: Few-shot generation asks a model to produce data from a new distribution after seeing only a small set of examples. Training draws on many sets whose distributions share underlying properties, such as characters from different alphabets or objects from different categories. The challenge is to use those few observations to capture the variation within a new set.

SCHA-VAE extends latent-variable models for sets into a fully hierarchical formulation. It uses attention to aggregate information from individual points into set-level context. This provides a hierarchical way to combine example-specific information with information describing the set as a whole, forming the model’s basis for few-shot generation.

The paper explores likelihood-based comparisons, iterative sampling, and out-of-distribution generalization without adaptation. Its results show that the hierarchical formulation better captures variation within sets when data are scarce. The authors position the method as a step toward large-scale few-shot generation, with a formulation compatible with current deep generative models, rather than claiming that this broader goal has already been completed.
icml-2022-scha-vae-hierarchical-context-.tldr: SCHA-VAE uses hierarchical latent variables and attention-based set aggregation to better capture variability for few-shot generation.

paragraphs: When classification involves many labels, ambiguity and class imbalance can make a single correct guess difficult. Top-K evaluation allows a model K guesses, but designing a corresponding training loss for deep networks remains challenging. This paper proposes a stochastic top-K hinge loss inspired by work on losses calibrated for top-K prediction.

The method smooths the top-K operator using the perturbed-optimizer framework. This places stochastic smoothing at the center of the loss design, connecting the training objective to the operation used to choose several candidate labels. The authors also introduce a simple variant intended for class-imbalanced data.

On balanced datasets, the proposed loss performs very well while requiring significantly less computation than the state-of-the-art top-K loss used for comparison. On a heavy-tailed dataset, the imbalanced variant significantly outperforms the evaluated baseline losses. Together, these findings support the approach as an efficient training objective for top-K classification, with a specific adjustment that helps in the reported imbalance setting.
icml-2022-stochastic-smoothing-of-the-to.tldr: A stochastically smoothed top-K hinge loss combines strong reported classification performance with lower computation and an effective imbalance variant.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization uses objective evaluations when gradients are unavailable. For nonsmooth convex problems, much previous work has focused on the total number of oracle calls. This paper also emphasizes iteration complexity: the number of successive optimization steps. The distinction matters because work performed within a step may be parallelized, whereas successive steps impose dependencies.

The authors propose a generic approach that builds zeroth-order algorithms from optimal first-order methods. It allows techniques developed for gradient-based optimization to be used as components in a black-box procedure for nonsmooth convex objectives. The resulting algorithms achieve optimal oracle complexity while retaining iteration complexity similar to first-order methods.

These two guarantees address different computational concerns: total evaluation effort and the number of sequential rounds. The iteration result makes it possible to exploit parallel computation to accelerate convergence. The paper also discusses extensions to stochastic optimization, saddle-point problems, and distributed optimization, showing how the approach connects to several related optimization settings.
icml-2022-the-power-of-first-order-smoot.tldr: A generic conversion of first-order methods yields black-box nonsmooth convex algorithms with optimal oracle complexity and favorable parallelizable iteration complexity.

paragraphs: UniRank addresses online ranking: choosing items from a collection of L candidates and assigning them to K webpage positions to maximize clicks. The learner repeatedly makes assignments and receives feedback. The paper proposes a generic bandit algorithm that handles multiple established click models, making the ranking method applicable across different descriptions of user clicking behavior.

Its regret guarantee follows from a pseudo-unimodality property on a graph whose nodes represent ordered sets of indistinguishable items. The main bound is O((L/Delta) log T), where T counts assignments and Delta is related to the reward gap between items. The guarantee relies on the condition that two items do not have identical attractiveness, making that distinction an explicit part of the result.

Experiments use real and synthetic datasets and compare UniRank with both specialized and generic learning algorithms. The reported finding is better regret performance than other generic algorithms. This supports the practical value of combining broad click-model coverage with a logarithmic-in-time regret guarantee under the stated attractiveness condition.
icml-2022-unirank-unimodal-bandit-algori.tldr: UniRank provides a generic online-ranking algorithm with logarithmic regret under a distinct-attractiveness condition and strong reported comparisons against generic alternatives.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter selection can be formulated as a bilevel problem, with one optimization problem nested inside another. The paper identifies a mismatch between many such applications and the guarantees available for existing gradient-based methods. Those guarantees require the lower-level problem to be smooth and strongly convex when upper-level variables are fixed, conditions that many tuning problems do not satisfy.

The authors develop VF-iDCA, a value-function-based difference-of-convex algorithm that allows inexactness. They establish sequential convergence and show that the algorithm can reach stationary solutions without the two lower-level assumptions for a broad class of hyperparameter-tuning applications. The guarantee concerns stationarity and applies to that class of problems.

Extensive experiments support the theoretical results and report superior hyperparameter-tuning performance for the proposed method. The significance is the connection between practical problem structure and available theory: more tuning formulations can receive a convergence guarantee without first requiring smoothness and strong convexity of their lower-level optimization problems.
icml-2022-value-function-based-differenc.tldr: VF-iDCA reaches stationary solutions for a broad class of bilevel tuning problems without requiring lower-level smoothness or strong convexity.

paragraphs: Hierarchical probabilistic models can contain many observations and local variables, making inference difficult. Sampling methods may struggle to scale, while variational inference can be inaccurate when its approximation family is too simple. Techniques such as importance-weighted variational inference can improve accuracy, but the paper notes difficulties with subsampling and high-dimensional models.

The proposed solution applies methods for tightening variational bounds separately to each group of local random variables. This creates a family of locally enhanced bounds for hierarchical models. Applying the improvements within lower-dimensional groups allows the method to use their strengths without treating the full collection of local variables as one high-dimensional problem.

The authors show that the approach naturally supports subsampling while providing unbiased gradients. They also report better results and more accurate posterior approximations than relevant baselines. The contribution combines two useful properties: stronger approximation objectives at the local level and a training procedure that can work with subsets of the data, addressing accuracy and scalability together.
icml-2022-variational-inference-with-loc.tldr: Locally tightened variational bounds improve hierarchical-model inference while supporting subsampling with unbiased gradients.
